# 06 — Fast Polynomial Algorithms

A polynomial is a finite coefficient array, but it is useful to think of it as
a compact description of size-indexed choices: $[x^k]A(x)$ is the answer for
total size $k$. This chapter explains why the fast operations work and when
their algebraic preconditions hold. It assumes your library already supplies
tested convolution and basic polynomial operations.

## 1. Multiplication is adding independent sizes

For $C(x)=A(x)B(x)$,

$$c_k=\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j. \tag{1}$$

Each summand chooses an $i$-sized object from $A$ and a $(k-i)$-sized object
from $B$. This “split a total” meaning is why convolution occurs in counting,
DP merging, and formal power series.

The transform idea is simple: evaluate polynomials at a specially chosen set of
points. At every point $z$, $(AB)(z)=A(z)B(z)$, so multiplication becomes
pointwise. An FFT uses complex roots of unity; an NTT uses roots of unity in a
finite field. Interpolation returns to coefficient form.

### Transform contract

For an NTT of length $L=2^s$ modulo prime $p$, we need $L\mid p-1$ so the
field has a primitive $L$th root of unity. The result length must cover every
possible degree, so $L\ge |A|+|B|-1$. For example,
$998244353=119\cdot2^{23}+1$ supports powers of two through $2^{23}$.

If the answer is modulo an arbitrary $m$, do not pretend one NTT prime computes
it. Convolve under one or more NTT-friendly primes, reconstruct the integer
coefficient by CRT (or use Garner to perform the same reconstruction directly
modulo $m$ when the bounded coefficients are nonnegative), then reduce. Garner
avoids storing a huge reconstructed integer; it does not remove the
reconstruction-range requirement. For signed coefficients, centered CRT must
also determine whether the representative means $c$ or $c-P$, where $P$ is the
product of auxiliary primes; a direct Garner residue needs the corresponding
sign correction modulo $m$. The number
of primes is determined by a proved bound on the *integer* coefficients: for a
signed coefficient of absolute value at most $B$, centered CRT needs a product
of moduli greater than $2B$. Three primes are a convention, not a proof.
Complex FFT instead needs coefficient splitting and a rounding-error bound.

## 2. Division: turn the high-degree end into a series inverse

Given $A=BQ+R$ with $\deg R<\deg B$, ordinary long division removes the
highest remaining term one at a time. Reversal makes those highest terms become
the low-degree terms of a formal power series, where inversion is fast. If
$\deg A<\deg B$, there is nothing to divide: return $Q=0,R=A$.

Let $k=\deg A-\deg B+1$. Define $\operatorname{rev}_k(F)$ by reading the
coefficients from $F$'s leading term downward, retaining the first $k$ and
padding with trailing zeros if fewer exist. Then

$$
\operatorname{rev}_k(Q)
\equiv \operatorname{rev}_k(A)\operatorname{rev}_k(B)^{-1}\pmod{x^k}. \tag{2}
$$

Why is this legal? The leading coefficient of $B$ becomes the constant
coefficient of $\operatorname{rev}(B)$; it can be inverted precisely when the
leading coefficient is nonzero in the coefficient field. Terms from $R$ land
beyond the first $k$ reversed coefficients and disappear modulo $x^k$. Reverse
the quotient back, then compute $R=A-BQ$.

This costs $O(M(n))$ with fast multiplication. It is a field operation. Over a
composite modulus a nonzero leading coefficient might not be invertible, so
this division contract can fail.

## 3. Product trees and multipoint evaluation

To evaluate $f$ at points $x_0,\ldots,x_{m-1}$, build a balanced tree. A leaf
stores $x-x_i$; an internal node stores the product of its children:

$$P_v(x)=\prod_{i\text{ below }v}(x-x_i).$$

At the root, replace $f$ by its remainder modulo $P_{root}$. A polynomial
remainder modulo $x-x_i$ is its value at $x_i$, so recursively passing the
remainder modulo each child reaches $f(x_i)$ at every leaf. This is the same
divide-and-conquer idea as a segment tree: a node stores the polynomial that
vanishes at all points in its interval.

If $\deg f=O(m)$, fast division at each level costs $O(M(m)\log m)$ in the
balanced case. For a higher-degree $f$, first reducing it modulo $P_{root}$
adds the cost of that division. For a small number of points, Horner's rule is
simpler and often faster; use a product tree only when the asymptotic saving
matters.

## 4. Interpolation reverses evaluation

Now suppose the points $x_i$ are pairwise distinct in the coefficient field and
the desired values $y_i$ are known. Let

$$P(x)=\prod_i(x-x_i).$$

The polynomial $P(x)/(x-x_i)$ vanishes at every $x_j$ except $x_i$. Dividing
it by its value there, $P'(x_i)$, creates a basis polynomial that is $1$ at
$x_i$ and $0$ at every other sample. Therefore

$$f(x)=\sum_i y_i\frac{P(x)}{(x-x_i)P'(x_i)}. \tag{3}$$

This formula is not magic: each summand is responsible for exactly one sample.
Evaluate $P'$ at all points via the product tree, place $w_i=y_i/P'(x_i)$ at
leaves, and merge children as

$$F_v=F_LP_R+F_RP_L.$$

At the root this is (3), in $O(M(n)\log n)$. If points repeat, $P'(x_i)=0$
and ordinary interpolation is undefined; repeated-value data needs the
stronger Hermite-interpolation problem.

For values at consecutive points $0,\ldots,n$, the denominators simplify to
$i!(-1)^{n-i}(n-i)!$. Prefix and suffix products of $(t-j)$ evaluate (3) at one
arbitrary $t$ in $O(n)$. Factorials must be invertible, so normally $n<MOD$.

## 5. Taylor shift: substitute $x+c$ in one convolution

We want the coefficients of $f(x+c)$, not just its value at one point. Expanding
each monomial gives

$$[x^k]f(x+c)=\sum_{i\ge k}a_i\binom ikc^{i-k}. \tag{4}$$

This says degree $i$ contributes to every lower degree $k$. Expand the binomial
coefficient and reverse the $a_i i!$ array; (4) becomes one convolution with
the array $c^j/j!$, followed by division by $k!$. If $n=\deg f$, put
$u_{n-i}=a_i i!$ and $v_j=c^j/j!$. Then

$$\frac{(u*v)_{n-k}}{k!}=
\sum_{i\ge k}a_i\binom ikc^{i-k},$$

so $(u*v)_{n-k}$ is $k!$ times the shifted coefficient of $x^k$; the final
division by $k!$ is essential. For example, if $f(x)=x^2$ and $c=1$, then the
convolution entries at indices $2,1,0$ are $1,2,2$, and division by
$0!,1!,2!$ gives the coefficients $1,2,1$ of $(x+1)^2$.
The reversal lines up $i-k$ as a convolution index. As with binomial transforms,
this needs the factorials through the working degree to be units; it is normally
used over a prime modulus larger than that degree.

## 6. Many factors: keep merge sizes balanced

For $\prod_i A_i(x)$, multiplying factors one after another repeatedly makes a
large polynomial absorb a tiny one. A divide-and-conquer product tree, or a
priority queue that merges the two smallest degrees, keeps products balanced.
For total output degree $N$, this is typically $O(M(N)\log k)$.

If the question only asks through degree $D$, truncate after each merge. In a
knapsack-style product such as $\prod_i(1+x^{w_i})$, coefficients above $D$
can never influence lower coefficients later, so retaining them only wastes
time and memory.

## 7. Failure checklist and sources

- Before an NTT, verify both the required length and the root-of-unity condition.
- Before a polynomial inverse, verify a nonzero/invertible constant term; before
  division, verify the leading coefficient condition instead.
- Normalize negative coefficients in the target ring.
- For CRT convolution, prove the reconstruction range covers a coefficient.
- Interpolation requires distinct sample points; consecutive-point formulas
  additionally need nonzero factorial denominators.
- Check a small product, quotient/remainder identity, and interpolation samples
  independently of the fast routine.
